passage: In the robotics room after school, Irawati ma'am held out the camp form. “Seats close on Friday, Uma. You built the best arm in the club.” Uma smiled too quickly. “June is busy. Family things.” The form stayed on the desk. At home that evening nobody asked, because Uma had said nothing; Papa only remarked how nice it would be to have an extra pair of hands at the shop all month. Uma nodded and kept stacking notebooks. Through June, Uma counted stock with a tight jaw, answered in single words, and once shut the cash drawer so hard that a customer jumped. “What's wrong with you?” asked Papa. “Nothing.” The family thought the summer had gone smoothly. Irawati ma'am glanced at the empty chair on the camp list and wondered why Uma never explained.

qa.q: By which day did the camp seats close?
What was Uma feeling while counting stock in June?
qa.a: Resentment: the tight jaw, one-word answers and the slammed drawer show anger that was never spoken.

qa.q: What could Uma have done instead, and why might it work?
qa.a: Uma could have told Papa what the camp meant and asked what the shop really needed, because then the family could look for a way to meet both needs instead of losing one silently.

qa.q: How does the summer look to Papa?
qa.a: Papa believes it went smoothly and does not know Uma gave up something important, so he cannot understand the short temper.

grounding: A student gives up the camp silently to avoid conflict, resentment builds and the family never learns the cost.

passage:
Dear Nitin,

You asked why I wasn't at the football camp in Goa. I told everyone it was "family stuff". The truth is simpler and worse.

Papa's bakery lost its delivery boy in May, and Mummy said, "It would help if you stayed." Not an order. Just tired. I didn't want a fight, so I said, "Okay, I'll skip the camp." I never told them the coach had picked me specially, or that scouts from the state team were coming.

So I've been delivering bread on the scooter for three weeks. Every morning I pass the ground where the others trained before leaving. And every morning I feel a little angrier, at nobody in particular. Yesterday I snapped at Papa over nothing. He looked confused.

They think I didn't mind. They don't know what I gave up. I'm starting to think that's my fault.

Joseph

qa.q: How long has Joseph been delivering bread?
What is Joseph feeling as each morning passes?
qa.a: Joseph feels growing resentment and anger, aimed at nobody in particular, along with some guilt.

qa.q: What approach might have worked better than saying yes silently?
qa.a: Telling the parents what the camp meant, including the scouts, and then looking for a middle option together, so any sacrifice is shared knowingly.

qa.q: How might Papa have experienced being snapped at over nothing?
qa.a: Papa was probably confused and a little hurt, not knowing about the camp or the hidden resentment behind it.

grounding: A letter shows a student giving up a camp without telling the family what it meant, avoiding conflict but growing resentful while the family never learns the cost.

passage:
Jaya, you want to know why I got so quiet that summer? Let me just say it.

I'm Shankar. My parents run a tea stall at the bus stand, and that year my uncle, who helped them, moved to Dubai. So when my school selected me for the state-level science camp, I knew what the answer would be before I asked. So I didn't ask. I threw the selection letter in my drawer and told my teacher I couldn't go.

My parents never knew. I worked the stall all May, pouring tea and counting coins, telling myself I was being a good son.

But inside, something went sour. I stopped studying science. I got annoyed at small things, like Amma asking me to fetch milk. Last month Amma found the letter while cleaning. She sat down on my bed and asked, "Why didn't you tell us?" I didn't have an answer that made sense.

qa.q: Where did Shankar put the selection letter?
How did Shankar feel inside during that summer?
qa.a: Shankar felt quietly bitter and resentful, which showed in losing interest in science and getting annoyed at small things.

qa.q: What might have happened if Shankar had shown the letter?
qa.a: The family might have found a way, like help from a neighbour or a shorter stay, and at least would have known what was being given up.

qa.q: How might Amma have felt finding the letter?
qa.a: Amma likely felt hurt and sad, realising her son had given up a chance without letting the family even consider it.

grounding: A spoken account of a student giving up a camp silently to avoid conflict, with resentment growing and the family never learning what was given up.
